text: Field Marshal Sam Hormusji Framji Jamshedji Manekshaw (3 April 1914 – 27 June 2008), also known as Sam Bahadur ("the Brave"), was an Indian Army general who served as the Chief of the Army Staff during the 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War and became the first Indian army officer to be promoted to the rank of field marshal. His military career spanned four decades, beginning with service in World War II. Manekshaw joined the first intake of the Indian Military Academy (IMA) at Dehradun in 1932, where he was selected as one of fifteen cadets and placed sixth in merit. He was commissioned into the 4th Battalion, 12th Frontier Force Regiment. During World War II, he was awarded the Military Cross for gallantry, particularly during the 1942 campaign at the Sittang River, where he led a counter-attack at Pagoda Hill despite 30% casualties and was severely wounded, surviving after being treated by an Australian surgeon who removed bullets from his lungs, liver, and kidneys and most of his intestines. After the war, he served in various staff roles, including at the Military Operations Directorate, and was promoted to colonel in 1952 and brigadier in 1957. Following the Partition of India in 1947, his unit became part of the Pakistan Army, and he was reassigned to the 8th Gorkha Rifles; Muhammad Ali Jinnah reportedly offered him a position in the Pakistani Army, which he refused. He served as commander of the 167 Infantry Brigade from 1952 to 1954, then as director of military training at Army Headquarters from 1954 to 1955. He was appointed commandant of the Defence Services Staff College in 1955 and later promoted to substantive major general in 1959. In 1961, he faced a politically motivated treason trial related to his refusal to remove British portraits from the college and his office, which was ultimately dismissed due to lack of evidence. The Sino-Indian War in 1962 led to his being accused in a politically motivated trial, though he was found innocent and thus could not participate in the conflict. In 1963, he was promoted to army commander and took over Western Command, then Eastern Command in 1964, where he played a key role in the 1967 Nathu La and Cho La clashes, marking India's first victory against a Chinese offensive. He was awarded the Padma Bhushan in 1968 for his response to insurgencies in Nagaland and Mizoram and became the seventh Chief of Army Staff in 1969. Under his leadership, Indian forces provided arms and ammunition to fight Pakistan during the 1971 Bangladesh War, which resulted in Bangladesh's independence in December 1971. He was awarded the Padma Vibhushan in 1972 for his services to the nation and promoted to field marshal in January 1973, becoming the first of only two officers to reach that rank, the other being K.M. Carriappa. He retired on 15 January 1973, celebrated as Army Day, and died on 27 June 2008 at the age of 94 due to respiratory problems. Manekshaw was born in Amritsar to Hormizd (1871–1964), a doctor, and Hilla, née Mehta (1885–1970), both Parsis who had moved from Valsad, Gujarat. The couple had four sons and two daughters, with Manekshaw being their fifth child and third son. He completed primary schooling in Punjab and studied at Sherwood College, Nainital for eight years, graduating in April 1932. He was initially assigned to the 2nd Battalion, Royal Scots before being posted to the 4th Battalion, 12th Frontier Force Regiment in Burma, where he qualified as a Higher Standard army interpreter in Pashto. He attended the eighth staff course at the Command and Staff College in Quetta in 1943 and served as brigade major of the Razmak Brigade until 1944. He was appointed to supervise the disarmament of over 10,000 Japanese prisoners of war during the Japanese surrender and later served as a staff officer to Field Marshal Sir Claude Auchinleck. He was one of three army officers representing India at the 1949 Karachi Conference, which resulted in the Karachi Agreement and the establishment of the Ceasefire Line (later the Line of Control), alongside Lt. Gen. S. M. Shrinagesh and Maj. Gen. KS Thimayya. He was promoted to substantive major on 4 February 1947 and appointed Grade 1 General Staff Officer (GSO1) in the Military Operations Directorate upon returning from Australia. He was promoted to brigadier in 1957 and later became commandant of the Infantry School at Mhow, where he led efforts to update outdated training manuals. He was also appointed colonel of the 8th Gorkha Rifles and the 61st Cavalry. In 1957, he attended a year-long higher command course at the Imperial Defence College in London. Upon returning, he was appointed GOC of the 26th Infantry Division in December 1957 with the acting rank of major general. During a visit to his division, Defence Minister Krishna Menon asked him about Chief of Army Staff K. S. Thimayya, to which Manekshaw replied that it was improper to evaluate his superior and stated that if Menon wanted to remove Thimayya, he could, but he would get another. This angered Menon. In 1961, after Major General Brij Mohan Kaul was appointed Chief of General Staff against Thimayya’s recommendation, Manekshaw opposed political interference in military affairs and was accused of sedition for not removing British portraits, leading to a court inquiry that exonerated him. The Sino-Indian War in 1962 led to his being unable to participate due to the court proceedings. In November 1962, Nehru asked him to take over IV Corps, and after explaining that the court action was a conspiracy and that his promotion had been delayed for nearly eighteen months, Nehru apologized. On 2 December 1962, Manekshaw was promoted to acting lieutenant general and appointed GOC of IV Corps at Tezpur. He concluded that poor leadership, particularly panicked withdrawals without soldier consent, had contributed to the corps' failure and ordered no more retreats without his written permission. He then began reorganizing the troops in the North-East Frontier Agency.

The Sino-Indian War broke out in 1962; Manekshaw was unable to participate due to court proceedings. The Indian Army was defeated in the war, and Kaul and Menon were primarily held responsible, both being sacked. In November 1962, Nehru asked Manekshaw to take over the command of IV Corps. Manekshaw told Nehru that the court action against him was a conspiracy and that his promotion had been due for nearly eighteen months; Nehru apologised. Shortly after, on 2 December 1962, Manekshaw was promoted to acting lieutenant general and appointed GOC of IV Corps at Tezpur. Soon after taking charge, Manekshaw concluded that poor leadership had significantly contributed to IV Corps' failure, identifying panicked withdrawals without allowing soldiers to fight back as the root cause of low morale. He ordered no more retreats without his written permission. His next task was to reorganise troops in the North-East Frontier Agency (NEFA), where he alleviated shortages of equipment, accommodation, and clothing. Analyst Srinath Raghavan noted that Corps Commander Manekshaw and COAS Jayanto Nath Chaudhuri delayed moving into NEFA until the end of 1963 to avoid provoking a new Chinese offensive. Promoted to substantive lieutenant general on 20 July 1963, Manekshaw was appointed army commander on 5 December, taking command of Western Command as GOC-in-C. Defence analyst Ajai Shukla, citing Anit Mukherjee, states that Western Command troops were reported to move from Punjab to Delhi after Nehru's death, seen as a precursor to a coup by the civilian establishment, while the army claimed it was for managing crowds at Nehru's funeral. As a result, on 16 November 1964, Manekshaw was transferred from Shimla to Calcutta as GOC-in-C Eastern Command, where he responded to insurgencies in Nagaland and Mizoram, for which he was awarded the Padma Bhushan in 1968. In 1967, five years after the 1962 war, China captured four critical posts in Sikkim—Nathu La, Jelep La, Sebu La, and Cho La—strategically valuable as they oversaw the Chicken's Neck, the narrow strip of land providing access to Northeast India. Major General Sagat Singh decided not to retreat following the Chinese attack; Manekshaw endorsed this initiative and remarked: "I am afraid they are enacting Hamlet without the Prince. I will now tell you how I intend to deal with this." The conflict ended in Indian victory following the Chinese withdrawal. Gen. P. P. Kumaramangalam retired as COAS in June 1969; Manekshaw was appointed eighth COAS on 8 June 1969. During his tenure, he was instrumental in stopping a plan to reserve quotas in the army for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, believing reservation would compromise the army's ethos and that all should have equal opportunity. In July 1969, during a visit to a battalion of the 8 Gorkha Rifles, Manekshaw asked an orderly if he knew the name of his chief; the orderly replied "Sam Bahadur" (lit. 'Sam the Brave'), which eventually became Manekshaw's nickname. During this period, there were suspicions that Manekshaw would lead a coup and impose martial law; Indira Gandhi asked him if he intended to do so, and he denied it. Once, an American diplomat, in the presence of Kenneth Keating, the US ambassador to India, asked Manekshaw when he would stage a coup; Manekshaw reportedly said, "As soon as General Westmoreland takes over your country." The Indo-Pakistani War of 1971 was sparked by the Bangladesh Liberation War, a conflict between dominant West Pakistanis and East Pakistanis, who were a majority but lacked representation. In 1970, East Pakistanis called for autonomy, which the Pakistani government failed to meet. In early 1971, secession gained momentum; in March, the Pakistan Armed Forces launched a campaign to suppress secessionists, including soldiers and police from East Pakistan. Thousands of East Pakistanis died, and nearly ten million refugees fled to West Bengal. In April, India decided to intervene militarily to create Bangladesh. During a cabinet meeting at the end of April, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi asked Manekshaw if he was prepared to go to war with Pakistan. He replied that most of his armoured and infantry divisions were deployed elsewhere, only twelve tanks were combat-ready, and they would compete for rail carriages with the grain harvest. He also noted that the Himalayan passes would open with the monsoon, leading to heavy flooding. After the cabinet left, Manekshaw offered to resign; Gandhi declined and instead sought his advice. He said he could guarantee victory if she allowed him to handle the conflict on his own terms and set a date for its initiation; Gandhi agreed. Following Manekshaw's strategy, the army launched several preparatory operations in East Pakistan, including training and equipping the Mukti Bahini, a local militia of Bengali nationalists. About three brigades of regular Bangladeshi troops were trained, and 75,000 guerrillas were trained and equipped with arms and ammunition. These forces were used to harass Pakistani Army forces in the lead-up to the war. The war officially began on 3 December 1971, when Pakistani aircraft bombed Indian Air Force bases in western India. Army Headquarters under Manekshaw's leadership formulated a strategy: II Corps under Lt. Gen. Tapishwar Narain Raina would enter from the west; IV Corps under Lt. Gen. Sagat Singh from the east; XXXIII Corps under Lt. Gen. Mohan L. Thapan from the north; and the 101 Communication Zone Area under Maj. Gen. Gurbax Singh from the northeast. This strategy was to be executed by Eastern Command under Lt. Gen. Jagjit Singh Aurora. Manekshaw instructed Lt. Gen. J.F.R. Jacob, chief of staff, Eastern Command, to inform the prime minister that troop movements were being issued. The following day, the Indian Navy and Air Force initiated full-scale operations on both eastern and western fronts. As the war progressed, India captured most strategic positions and isolated Pakistani forces, who began to surrender or withdraw. The UN Security Council assembled on 4 December 1971 to discuss the situation. After lengthy discussions on 7 December, the United States proposed a resolution for an "immediate cease-fire and withdrawal of troops," which was supported by the majority but vetoed twice by the USSR; due to Pakistani atrocities in Bengal, the UK and France abstained. On 8 December, a C141 American cargo plane was seen unloading arms and equipment at Karachi. Manekshaw prevented further supplies by summoning the military attaché at the US embassy in India and asking him to stop the drops, which were in contravention of US public policy. On 9 December 1971, Manekshaw delivered his first radio message to Pakistani troops: "Indian forces have surrounded you. Your Air Force is destroyed. You have no hope of any help from them. Chittagong, Chalna and Mangla ports are blocked. Nobody can reach you from the sea. Your fate is sealed. The Mukti Bahini and the people are all prepared to take revenge for the atrocities and cruelties you have committed...Why waste lives? Don't you want to go home and be with your children? Do not lose time; there is no disgrace in laying down your arms to a soldier. We will give you the treatment befitting a soldier." Manekshaw addressed Pakistani troops by radio on 9, 11, and 15 December, assuring them of honourable treatment if they surrendered. The last two broadcasts were replies to messages from Pakistani commanders Maj. Gen. Rao Farman Ali and Lt. Gen. Amir Abdullah Khan Niazi to their troops. These broadcasts demoralised the Pakistani forces and convinced them of the futility of further resistance, leading to their decision to surrender. On 11 December, Ali requested a ceasefire from the UN, but it was not authorised by President Yahya Khan, and fighting continued. After several discussions and consultations and subsequent attacks by Indian forces, Khan decided to stop the war to avoid further casualties. The actual decision to surrender was taken by Niazi on 15 December and conveyed to Manekshaw through the US Consul General in Dhaka via Washington. Manekshaw replied that he would stop the war only if Pakistani troops surrendered to Indian counterparts by 9 AM on 16 December. The deadline was extended to 3 PM on the same day at Niazi's request, and the instrument of surrender was formally signed on 16 December 1971 by Lt. Gen. Amir Abdullah Khan Niazi. When the prime minister asked Manekshaw to go to Dhaka to accept the surrender, he declined, stating that the honour should go to GOC-in-C Eastern Command, Lt. Gen. Jagjit Singh Aurora. Concerned about maintaining discipline, Manekshaw issued strict instructions forbidding looting and rape and stressed the need to respect and stay away from women. As a result, according to Singh, cases of looting and rape were negligible. While addressing his troops, Manekshaw was quoted as saying: "When you see a Begum (Muslim woman), keep your hands in your pockets, and think of Sam." The war lasted 12 days and resulted in 93,000 Pakistani soldiers taken prisoner, ending with the unconditional surrender of East Pakistan and the creation of Bangladesh. In addition to the prisoners of war (POWs), Pakistan suffered 6,000 casualties against India's 2,000. After the war, Manekshaw ensured good conditions for the POWs, but was criticised for treating them like "sons in law" by the cabinet. Singh recounts that in some cases he addressed them personally and talked to them privately, with just his aide-de-camp for company, while they shared a cup of tea. He made provisions for prisoners to receive copies of the Quran, celebrate festivals, and receive letters and parcels from loved ones. However, he did not want them returned to Pakistan until a peace agreement was concluded, as the POWs numbered about four divisions and could be deployed for another war. The Pakistani POWs remained in captivity for several years, used as leverage for Pakistan to officially recognise Bangladesh. Manekshaw was India's official representative for negotiations held on 28 November 1972 to demarcate the Line of Control in Kashmir after the war; Pakistan's representative was General Tikka Khan. The talks broke down due to disagreements over control of Thako Chak and Kaiyan (in Pakistan's Chicken's Neck), Chhamb, and Tortuk. The second round of talks from 5 to 7 December resolved these issues. After the war, Indira Gandhi decided to promote Manekshaw to the rank of field marshal and appoint him as chief of defence staff (CDS). However, after objections from navy and air force commanders, the appointment was dropped due to concerns that the smaller forces would be neglected and that bureaucrats feared reduced influence over defence issues. Though Manekshaw was to retire in June 1972, his term was extended by six months, and "in recognition of outstanding services to the Armed Forces and the nation," he was promoted to field marshal on 1 January 1973. The first Indian Army officer to receive this rank, he was formally conferred in a ceremony at Rashtrapati Bhavan on 3 January. For his service to India, President VV Giri awarded Manekshaw the Padma Vibhushan in 1972. Manekshaw retired from active service on 15 January 1973 (celebrated as Army Day in India) after a career of nearly four decades. He moved with his family to Coonoor, the civilian town next to Wellington Cantonment, where he had served as commandant of the Defence Services Staff College. Popular with Gorkha soldiers, Nepal fêted Manekshaw as an honorary general of the Nepalese Army in 1972. In 1977, he was awarded the Order of Tri Shakti Patta First Class, an order of knighthood of the Kingdom of Nepal by King Birendra. Following his service in the Indian Army, Manekshaw served as an independent director on the board and, in a few cases, as chairman of several companies, including Bombay Burmah Trading Corporation, Britannia Industries, and Escorts Limited. In May 2007, Gohar Ayub, son of Pakistani Field Marshal Ayub Khan, claimed that Manekshaw had sold Indian Army secrets to Pakistan during the 1965 Indo-Pakistani War for 20,000 rupees; the Indian defence establishment dismissed the accusations. Although Manekshaw was conferred the rank of field marshal in 1973, he was not given his full allowances until 2007, when President A. P. J. Abdul Kalam met him in Wellington and presented him with a cheque for ₹1.3 crore (equivalent to ₹3.9 crore or US$460,000 in 2023)—his arrears of pay for over 30 years. Manekshaw was critical of politicians and civilian bureaucrats, frequently mocking them, for example, asking whether political masters in charge of national defence could distinguish a mortar from a motor, a gun from a howitzer, or a guerrilla from a gorilla—though many in the past had resembled the latter. Manekshaw visited hospitalised soldiers during the Kargil War and was cited by COAS Ved Prakash Malik, the commander during the war, as his icon. Manekshaw married Silloo Bode on 22 April 1939 in Bombay. The couple had two daughters. Manekshaw died of complications from pneumonia at the Military Hospital in Wellington, Tamil Nadu, at 12:30 a.m. on 27 June 2008 at the age of 94. Reportedly, his last words were "I'm okay!" He was buried at the Parsi cemetery in Udhagamandalam (Ooty), Tamil Nadu, with military honours, adjacent to his wife's grave. His funeral lacked governmental representation, which the media argued reflected the civilian establishment's apathy towards the military, fearing a military coup if the military became too popular. A national day of mourning was not declared, though this was not a breach of protocol, as such commemoration is customary for a leader of national importance. Bangladesh did pay tribute to Manekshaw on his death. He was survived by two daughters and three grandchildren. Manekshaw was charismatic and known for his charm. He was often described as a gentleman. Like others of his generation, his British army background gave him a fondness for English habits, such as drinking whisky and wearing his handlebar moustache. His Parsi background is sometimes attributed as a factor in his ambition and success. He commanded great loyalty from his troops, particularly the Gorkhas, due to his reputation for personal bravery, fairness, and avoidance of punishments. He came into conflict with politicians because he stood up to their unreasonable or unethical demands and feared their popularity might lead to a military coup. He dealt with such demands through sarcasm, which was recognised by figures such as Indira Gandhi. Manekshaw also advocated for better strategies than those developed by the civilian establishment, a trait rarely found in the military brass today, according to Admiral Arun Prakash. Throughout his military career, he was awarded the Military Cross in 1942 for gallantry in Burma during World War II at the battle of Pagoda Hill, the Padma Bhushan in 1968, and the Padma Vibhushan in 1972 for exceptional service. Vijay Diwas (lit. Victory Day) is celebrated on 16 December every year.

He often came into conflict with politicians because he stood up to their unreasonable or unethical demands and feared a military coup due to his popularity, which they disliked. He addressed politicians' demands through sarcasm, a style recognized by figures such as Indira Gandhi. Manekshaw did not hesitate to advocate for better strategies than those developed by the civilian establishment, a trait rarely found in the military brass today, according to Admiral Arun Prakash. He was awarded the Military Cross in 1942 for gallantry in Burma during World War II at the battle of Pagoda Hill against the Japanese. He received the Padma Bhushan in 1968 and the Padma Vibhushan in 1972 for his exceptional service. Vijay Diwas, celebrated annually on 16 December, honors the victory achieved under Manekshaw's leadership in 1971. On 16 December 2008, a postage stamp depicting Manekshaw in his field marshal's uniform was released by then President Pratibha Patil. The Manekshaw Centre in the Delhi Cantonment is named after him and was inaugurated by the President of India on 21 October 2010; the biannual Army Commanders' conference is held there. The Manekshaw parade ground in Bengaluru is also named after him, where Republic Day celebrations in Karnataka take place annually. A flyover bridge in Ahmedabad's Shivranjeeni area was named after him in 2008 by then Chief Minister of Gujarat, Narendra Modi. In 2014, a granite statue was erected in his honour at Wellington in the Nilgiris district, near the Manekshaw Bridge on the Ooty–Coonoor road, which was named after him in 2009; his statue is also located on the Maneckji Mehta Road in Pune Cantonment. The Centre for Land Warfare Studies publishes its research papers in a collection called the Manekshaw Papers as a tribute. Manekshaw has been portrayed in film and fiction: Vicky Kaushal played the role of Manekshaw in the 2023 biopic Sam Bahadur, and he is featured conversing with his Pakistani adversary and former Burma war colleague Tiger Niazi in Salman Rushdie's novel Midnight's Children, in the chapter entitled "Sam and the Tiger". In 1970, the Armed Forces, particularly the Army, gained the opportunity for the first time to have their pay determined by the Pay Commission, which set pay levels for all government employees; armed forces had not been considered for the 1st and 2nd Pay Commissions but were to be considered for the 3rd Pay Commission. Manekshaw convinced the government to apply the 3rd Pay Commission's recommendations for military personnel and established pay scales proportionate to their service conditions (termed hazard pay), a practice that continues today. His strategies during the 1971 war are considered precursors to the Indian Cold Start military doctrine, which calls for integrated offensive attacks. Formulated with his deputies Aurora and Singh, Manekshaw's shock and awe tactic of deploying IV Corps, which was geographically disadvantaged, significantly contributed to the military victory. Analysts consider Manekshaw and Aurora to have created a Blitzkrieg-style warfare that was even more rapid. Defence analyst Robert M. Citino noted that the 1971 campaign was impressively fast but took too long to mobilize units, had crude logistics, and could have faced problems without an air force in East Pakistan; Manekshaw stated that comparing the campaign to Rommel's would be ridiculous. General André Beaufre, a French military theorist, was invited by Manekshaw to analyze the 1971 war; he had previously observed the Battles of Chumb and Basantar from the Pakistani side. Beaufre concluded that Indian operations on the Eastern Front were maneuver warfare, but operations in and around the Shakargarh bulge were too slow. On 12 October 1966, while on a flight from Delhi to Kolkata, Manekshaw was a co-passenger with William K. Hitchcock, the Consul General of the USA in Kolkata. During the flight, Manekshaw discussed the need for greater military involvement in Kashmir and criticized COAS Chaudhuri's decision not to deploy the 300,000 Indian soldiers of Eastern Command in the 1965 War due to fear of a Chinese offensive. He also expressed concerns over India's dependence on Soviet defence equipment and stated he would have advocated for a more American-friendly stance on the Vietnam War if he had had more power. Manekshaw advocated for a strong domestic defence industrial base and procurement reforms to shorten the long order and delivery cycles of the Indian Armed Forces. He was a critic of defence equipment imports and overreliance on the Soviet Union and its successor state, Russia. During the 1971 War, he managed to urgently procure equipment to achieve numerical superiority and raise new divisions, though he could not implement lasting procurement reforms. After being convinced by Brigadier Bhawani Singh on the need for special operations, Manekshaw approved the plans for the Chachro Raid, which the brigadier had drawn up himself. The raid captured 13,000 square kilometres (5,000 sq mi) of Pakistani territory up to Umerkot in Sindh province and is considered by analysts to be the most successful operation by an Indian special operations unit. While responding to the insurgency in Mizoram in 1966, Manekshaw implemented the policy of merging small villages (termed spatialisation) as a counter-insurgency tool. The policy aimed to prevent insurgents from hiding in sparsely populated villages, enabling safer civilian and military operations. By forcing insurgents to operate in uninhabited areas, they were denied access to food and supplies; the army had to patrol a smaller area and avoided high-casualty urban warfare.
